Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk (right) is welcomed by Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky and his wife Olena Zelenska during a Carpathian 8 Summit in Bukovel, western Ukraine, Friday. Photo - AP WARSAW (AP): Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned on Thursday that Russia is planning hybrid strikes with drones or rockets on European countries supporting Ukraine, among them Poland. Russia will pretend the attacks are “accidental” in order to “paralyse or at least weaken the motivation of NATO countries” to rush to the defence of the member state coming under attack, Tusk said in a speech to the Polish parliament. “There is a real risk that drones or other types of projectiles will enter the territory of one or several countries on the eastern flank and even cause destruction,” Tusk warned. “The official narration will be that it’s an accident and there is no reason for NATO to think about a response,” he added. He said Russia was more dangerous because it was increasingly using jet-powered drones, which fly higher and faster and thus are more difficult to detect by air defence before reaching their targets. Tusk has been for months warning that Russia might be preparing a more serious hybrid attack against a NATO country. His warnings have got increasingly specific as he received intelligence from NATO, Ukrainian and US secret services, including the CIA, he said. In recent days, Tusk has said Russia was now focusing on attacking border crossings between Ukraine and its European neighbours in order to disrupt delivery lines to Ukraine. Four such incidents happened on Poland’s border with Ukraine in the past week and several others took place in the last weeks on Ukraine’s border with Moldova. Tusk said at the moment Russia was not ready for any peace talks “without the total capitulation of Ukraine”. “They are convinced the winter will be tragically critical for Ukraine,” Tusk said. He said last winter Poland stepped in with deliveries when Ukraine’s energy infrastructure came under attack, but if border crossings are destroyed, it will be much harder for Warsaw to offer such help this upcoming winter. “Russia’s goal is to destroy as much as possible the economy and logistics of Ukraine,” Tusk said, adding that intelligence indicates continuous attacks of “very high frequency and intensity” on six main Ukrainian cities should be expected in the near future. Tusk announced on Thursday he would travel to Ukraine overnight to Friday, in what can be seen as an act of defiance against Russia after European leaders narrowly escaped a drone strike on a train near the Polish-Ukrainian border on Sunday. Officials usually keep their travel plans to Ukraine secret for security reasons. In Kyiv, he said he would discuss with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy how to defend against the new types of drones as well as discuss with partners including Slovakia about further sanctions against Russia. On Thursday, US President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that “major progress is being made toward establishing a US Army base in Poland” after a US delegation was in Poland last week to visit several possible locations. “If this happens, the location will be announced very soon,” Trump wrote. “This will be a historic step for our Great US-Polish Alliance.” Poland has for years sought to host a permanent US base as a strong guarantee of its security in the face of the rising Russian threat. Poland’s high defence spending and major US arms purchases have persuaded the Trump administration to consider putting a permanent base in Poland even as it reorganises and reduces its overall military presence in Europe. In May, the US unexpectedly withdrew troops from the total of around 10,000 stationed in Poland, causing confusion among European allies and nervousness in Warsaw. But officials in both Poland and the US soon said the withdrawal was temporary and Poland was not expected to suffer from the US troop reorganisation. https://www.natureworldnews.com/articles.text: Large dogs show faster molecular aging than small dogs, and one of the clearest signs is the loss of chemical tags that normally keep ancient "jumping genes" quiet, according to a study of nearly 900 pet dogs published Oct. 8 in the journal Science. The work, led by researchers at Arizona State University and part of the Dog Aging Project, offers a possible molecular explanation for why a Great Dane rarely reaches 10 while a Chihuahua can live about twice as long.Giant breeds lost about 35% more of these chemical tags per year on a major family of jumping genes than small breeds, Arizona State University reported. The researchers also found that dogs whose molecular age ran ahead of their actual age were more likely to die within the following two years.For dog owners, the findings do not change care advice today. But they point to a measurable biological process behind a pattern every veterinarian knows, and they may help researchers test whether aging can be slowed in dogs and, eventually, people.Jumping Genes and Their Chemical LeashJumping genes, known to scientists as transposable elements, are stretches of DNA that can copy themselves and insert the copies elsewhere in the genome. They are ancient genetic hitchhikers — and they make up a large share of mammal DNA, including human DNA.Cells keep most of them switched off with methyl groups, small chemical tags attached to DNA that block the cell's machinery from reading a stretch of code. Scientists call the full pattern of these tags the methylome, and it shifts in predictable ways as animals age.The study found that aging in dogs comes with a widespread loss of methylation, especially on transposable elements. The most affected class was LINE-1, a family of jumping genes, with more than 40% of LINE-1-associated regions losing methylation with age, according to ASU. When LINE-1 elements lose that chemical leash, they can become active again, copy themselves and damage DNA, processes linked to genome instability, inflammation and cancer."This is one of the clearest molecular signatures we've seen," said Blaise Mariner, an ASU researcher and author on the study. Senior author Noah Snyder-Mackler, a professor in ASU's School of Life Sciences, said big dogs "were aging a little bit faster per year of life than small dogs," as quoted by Live Science.Inside the Dog Aging Project DataThe researchers measured methylation in blood samples from pet dogs enrolled in the Dog Aging Project, a long-term study based at the University of Washington that has enrolled about 55,000 dogs whose owners complete health surveys and submit samples. The sample covered roughly 120 breeds, according to Nature's news report.Reported sample sizes differ slightly. Nature and Live Science put the number at 894 dogs, while ASU's release says 864. Nature World News was unable to access the Science paper directly to confirm the final figure.The team built an epigenetic clock, a statistical model that estimates a dog's age from its methylation pattern, which predicted age to within about a year. Dogs whose clock age ran older than their calendar age had a higher risk of death in a two-year follow-up period.The study also found sex differences. Nature reported that male dogs accumulated age-related changes faster than females, even when neutered young. ASU said LINE-1 elements on the X chromosome were more methylated in males than females, a result Brianah McCoy, who co-led the work as a doctoral researcher at ASU, called unexpected.Borbála Turcsán, who studies dog cognition and behavior at Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest and was not involved in the work, called the findings fascinating. "It provides a molecular background for something we also observe at a behavioural level," she told Nature.Limits of the Evidence So FarThe central limitation — one the researchers acknowledge — is that the results show an association, not cause and effect. ASU's release says more research is needed to determine whether jumping-gene activity drives aging or simply results from it, and Live Science notes that the jumping-gene link to faster aging in big dogs remains a hypothesis.The clock also explains only part of the variation between dogs. "What we really want to know is, what explains the rest of that variation?" Snyder-Mackler told Live Science. The researchers measured methylation in blood immune cells, which may not reflect every tissue in the body.Snyder-Mackler has suggested a possible trade-off in which rapid growth in large breeds, shaped by breeding for size, comes at the expense of body maintenance. That idea, too, is a hypothesis rather than a finding of this study.ASU's release does not list funding sources. The Dog Aging Project has historically been supported by the National Institute on Aging, but readers should check the published paper for the funding statement.Meaning for Dog Owners and Human Aging ResearchThe findings do not mean owners of large dogs should change food, exercise or veterinary care based on this study. Standard advice, including regular checkups, keeping dogs lean and watching for age-related disease, remains the best guidance, and owners with concerns should talk with their veterinarian.The larger value is scientific. Dogs share homes, environments and many diseases with people, and their shorter lives let researchers follow aging across a whole lifespan. "Our work suggests that transposable elements may be a fundamental part of the aging process across mammals," Snyder-Mackler said in the ASU release.If that holds up, jumping genes could become a target for therapies, though any such treatment is far from reality. The Dog Aging Project is still enrolling dogs, and the team plans to follow them longer to build better predictive models.The bottom line is that big dogs appear to age faster at the molecular level, with jumping genes losing their chemical restraints sooner. Whether that process causes shorter lives, or simply tracks them, is the next question researchers need to answer.What Readers Want to KnowWhy do big dogs have shorter lives?Researchers have long linked large size to shorter lifespans in dogs. This study suggests big dogs age faster at the molecular level, including faster loss of chemical tags on jumping genes.What are jumping genes?They are stretches of DNA, called transposable elements, that can copy themselves and move around the genome. Cells normally keep them silent with chemical tags called methyl groups.How many dogs were studied?Nature and Live Science report 894 dogs from about 120 breeds in the Dog Aging Project. Arizona State University's release gives 864.Does the study prove jumping genes cause aging?No. It shows an association. Researchers say more work is needed to find out whether jumping-gene activity drives aging or results from it.Should owners of large dogs change their care?Not based on this study. Regular veterinary checkups and keeping dogs at a healthy weight remain standard advice.Can my dog join the Dog Aging Project?The project is still enrolling dogs. Owners can check the Dog Aging Project's website for eligibility.
